column3: A collective confession of wrongdoing before the Lord gives a broad afterlife echo of the focus.
It links present blindness to being still more astray in the hereafter, extending the focus's path-and-consequence frame.
Its lack of any path after God's misguidance is only a general counterpart to the focus's human-led error.
The immediately preceding utterance regrets not obeying God and the messenger, directly setting up the contrary obedience in the focus.
A nearby warning of doubled punishment does not develop obedience to leaders or misguidance.
It directly warns that obeying the majority can lead one away from God's path, closely clarifying the focus's failed obedience.
An invocation before judgment has only the shared setting of a people speaking to their Lord.
It warns against following a people who went astray and led many astray, a close leader-and-follower pattern.
Those who set up rivals lead people away from God's path, supplying a related source of misguidance.
A post-punishment confession of sin and appeal for escape parallels the focus's retrospective speech without its leaders.
Nearby obedience to God and His messenger is an alternative model, but the domestic ruling is not about misguiding authority.
It identifies the leading criminals of each town and their schemes, adding the social prominence of corrupt leaders.
The people's refusal to follow a messenger calls that following misguidance, but does not concern following chiefs.
The immediate continuation asks doubled punishment and curse for those leaders, completing the focus's accusation.
Its domestic regulation only shares incidental vocabulary for obedience, path, and greatness.
A later regretful appeal to the Lord adds little beyond the earlier collective confession.
The command not to obey disbelievers provides a clear contrary norm to the focus's misplaced obedience.
The statement of greater punishment does not add an authority, path, or confession theme.
Moses describes Pharaoh and his elite as leading people from God's path, a related elite-led misguidance pattern.
The next local warning about harming Moses does not materially develop the focus's leader-follower claim.
It describes people barring others from God's path, though without the focus's obedience or afterlife confession.
A grateful speech after deliverance has only a generic collective address to God.
Its local command for sound speech follows the confession sequence and redirects the community's conduct.
At judgment, the question whether false objects led servants astray directly probes responsibility for misguidance.
A collective acknowledgment in punishment of the Lord's decree parallels the focus's communal eschatological voice.
It calls those gathered toward Hell most astray in path, a broad judgment-day parallel.
God's knowledge of who strays and who is guided supplies a general frame for the focus's claim of being led astray.
The believers' declaration that they heard and obeyed God and the messenger is the direct corrective counterpart to obeying chiefs.
The local continuation joins obedience to God and the messenger with success, sharply contrasting the focus's failed allegiance.
The imperative to obey God and the messenger supplies the alternative authority, though it is already established locally.
It models a speech of contentment with God and the messenger but does not address misguidance by leaders.
A wrongdoer on the Day of Judgment regrets not taking a way with the messenger, closely paralleling retrospective regret over allegiance.
A family accusation that a father is astray does not illuminate the focus's authority and consequence pattern.
The creation statement has no material connection to the focus.
A question about return after punishment shares the afterlife setting but not the focus's causal claim.
It makes obedience to the messenger the route to guidance, directly contrasting the focus's obedience that led astray.
The arrogance of Aad is not developed as following leaders or losing the path.
Divine guidance after being lost is only a distant individual counterpart to the collective misguidance in the focus.
Its command to obey God and the messenger reinforces the alternative allegiance, but is redundant with earlier parallels.
It warns against following desire lest it lead from God's path, adding a nonhuman source of misleading obedience.
The account of a destroyed town has no substantive link to the focus.
It places those disputing the Hour in distant misguidance, adding an eschatological path frame without leadership.
It distinguishes guidance and misguidance as bearing on each person, qualifying the focus's attribution of blame.
The hardship of the Day for disbelievers is too general to add to the focus.
Choosing a path to the Lord is a broad positive path image, not a leader-follower counterpart.
The legal procedure and incidental error vocabulary do not clarify the focus.
The speaker says another led him away after remembrance, giving a close individual analogue to the focus's accusation.
It warns believers that obeying a hostile group can reverse their faith, directly showing the danger of misplaced obedience.
Blocking people from God's path lacks the focus's relation of obedience to leaders.
The destruction of deniers does not add a relevant connection.
The recording of every small and great matter is unrelated to the focus's theme.
This narrative confrontation does not illuminate authority, path, or collective regret.
It warns that obeying disbelievers brings reversal and loss, a close but now redundant obedience-to-misguidance parallel.
The darkened faces of arrogant liars add only a broad punishment image.
Arrogance and harmful plotting do not establish the leader-follower relation in the focus.
The reaction to news of a daughter has no relevant connection.
It calls the believing community to obey God and the messenger, reinforcing the proper authority in contrast to the focus.
The divided faces and punishment for unbelief offer only a general afterlife consequence.
God's knowledge of those astray and guided provides a concise classification of the path condition named in the focus.
The social reaction to a daughter's birth is unrelated to the focus.
A group seeks to lead believers astray, supplying another direct account of people acting as misleaders.
The condemned collectively confess that they were astray, closely echoing the focus's post-punishment admission.
The acceptance of spending freely or unwillingly does not add to the focus.
The appeal to ancestral custom and following forebears is a direct structural parallel to obeying elders and chiefs.
The marriage prohibition shares only an incidental path term.
The resurrection objection does not clarify the focus.
It joins rejection and barring from God's path with far misguidance, a broad outcome parallel.
A generic cry of regret adds little after the earlier Garden confessions.
The comparison of religious service and striving in God's path is not about the focus's misguiding authorities.
A believing response to a caller offers a distant positive counterpart without a leader-misguidance dimension.
Satan is called a clear misleading enemy, but the narrative does not concern the focus's human leaders.
Those blamed at judgment acknowledge leading others astray as they themselves strayed, an especially close responsibility parallel.
The command to fight in God's path and God's attributes do not develop the focus.
The boast of wealth and children gestures toward elite arrogance but not obedient followers or misguidance.
Its ethical distinction among People of the Book has no material relation to the focus.
A believers' prayer for protection from punishment lacks the focus's authority and path themes.
Wrongdoers follow their desires without knowledge, adding a close account of misguided following even without human chiefs.
The announcement of a lost cup has no relevant connection.
Pharaoh makes his people follow him and they obey, a clear ruler-follower example with culpable outcome.
The messengers' assertion that their Lord knows does not develop the focus.
The unstable person and the absence of a path after divine misguidance offer a broad path parallel.
The prayer expressing fear before Pharaoh is not about followers being misled.
It says people turn others from God's path, but does not portray obedience to their authority.
The youths' prayer for mercy and right guidance is not a close counterpart.
The repeated command to obey God and the messenger reinforces the focus's missing proper allegiance.
The return to the Lord has no relevant leader or misguidance element.
The description of an obeyed messenger does not address wrongful obedience.
The praise of the Lord's fulfilled promise does not illuminate the focus.
The fighting command uses God's path in a different sense from the focus's way of guidance.
The condemned say that criminals led them astray, a direct and concise parallel to the focus's accusation.
The destruction statement has no connection to authority or misguidance.
God's knowledge of who is better guided is a marginal path parallel after stronger guidance verses.
The statement about an Arabic Quran is unrelated to the focus.
Seeking judgment from false authority while Satan seeks to lead them far astray closely extends the focus's wrongful allegiance.
The brief statement of loss has no material thematic link.
Satan beautifies a people's deeds and bars them from the path, a related account of an external misleader.
Its doctrinal warning and punishment do not develop the focus's leader-follower misguidance.
Pharaoh and his forces act arrogantly while denying return, adding an elite and accountability setting only indirectly.
The account of deceptive professions and textual distortion touches corrupt influence but not the focus's direct pattern.
The declaration that none can guide whom God leaves astray provides a theological boundary for the focus's human attribution.
Those who were followed disown their followers when punishment is seen, directly extending the focus's failed reliance on leaders.
Followers regret their allegiance and wish to disown those they followed, an exact counterpart to the focus's remorse.
The refusal to follow revelation in favor of ancestral practice gives a foundational parallel to obeying elders.
Appeal to what forefathers practiced supplies another compact instance of inherited allegiance overriding guidance.
People justify inherited wrongdoing by appeal to their fathers, a related mechanism of uncritical following.
Later nations in the Fire identify earlier ones as having led them astray and ask their doubled punishment, an especially close parallel.
The former group rejects the followers' attempt to transfer blame, qualifying the focus's accusation of leaders.
Taking religious authorities as lords names a direct form of misplaced human authority.
Pharaoh's people follow his command, which is explicitly not rightly guided, a close ruler-follower counterpart.
Pharaoh leads his people into the Fire, matching the focus's final consequence of following a chief.
The weak ask the arrogant in the Hereafter whether their former followers can be relieved of punishment, directly paralleling the focus's scene.
Satan denies coercive authority over those who answered his call and forbids mutual blame, sharply qualifying responsibility for misleading leadership.
Misleaders bear burdens for those they lead astray, adding an explicit accountability principle for the focus's leaders.
Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide them, a direct concise ruler-and-path parallel.
Regret over taking a particular companion complements the next candidate's statement that this companion led one astray.
Leaders who call to the Fire provide a direct structural analogue to the chiefs named in the focus.
Disbelievers invite believers to follow their way while falsely offering to bear their sins, a related deceptive-authority pattern.
The appeal to following forefathers despite contrary guidance closely parallels obedience to inherited elders.
The oppressed blame the arrogant for preventing their faith, a close post-judgment leader-follower dispute.
The arrogant deny having turned followers from guidance, preserving the contrary reading on responsibility.
The oppressed answer that the leaders' hidden plotting and commands caused disbelief, directly elaborating the focus's accusation.
Satan is said to have led many generations astray, adding a broad external-misleader counterpart.
The condemned question one another in the Fire, opening a closely related exchange of blame.
The accused deny having authority over the others, providing an explicit counterpoint to the focus's causal attribution.
The accused admit leading others astray because they themselves were astray, an exact recursive misguidance parallel.
Both groups share punishment, reinforcing joint accountability rather than blame transfer alone.
The weak in the Fire tell the arrogant that they were their followers and ask for relief, a very close parallel to the focus.
The arrogant answer that all are in the Fire under God's judgment, completing the shared-accountability exchange.
The condemned ask to be shown the humans and jinn who led them astray so they may abase them, directly echoing blame toward misleaders.
A community explicitly follows the tracks of its fathers despite a warner, closely matching the focus's appeal to elders.
Turning from remembrance results in a devilish companion, offering an alternative account of a misleading guide.
Those companions turn people from the path while the people think themselves guided, closely explaining misled obedience.
Some promise obedience to those who hate revelation, a direct but narrower example of wrongful human allegiance.
Their end is tied to following what angers God and disliking what pleases Him, supplying a consequence for corrupt allegiance.
Satan first commands disbelief and then disowns the follower, a compact analogy to unreliable misleaders.
The people of the Blaze admit that hearing or reasoning would have kept them from the Fire, contrasting the focus's failed obedience.
Noah says his people disobeyed him and followed one whose wealth and children only increased loss, a leader-following counterpart.
